articles.title: Bluesky blocks links to leaked DHS employee data as government seeks takedowns
articles.author: Zack Whittaker
articles.content:
Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.

Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collectiveDDoSecretswere marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outletsbroke the newsthat Homeland Security had been hacked.

TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked datasets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.”

Bluesky did not respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. West Coast business hours about the blocks. A Bluesky spokespersontold Wiredthat the exposed data violates itscommunity guideline rules, but chose to block the link rather than taking down the posts. (We’ll update if we hear back.)

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.

“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.

Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.

Asearch site, dubbed Icepick, made by journalistmaia arson crimewno longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” whichgenerally meansthat the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.

Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.”

CentralNic, which hosts the domain name, did not respond to a request for comment from TechCrunch about the takedown or whether it was instructed to do so by a government demand. ZeroFox also did not respond to a request for comment.

The Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up regarding the takedown notice affecting Icepick’s website.

Crimew also made a locally hosted version of the data, allowing anyone to access it on their own computer.

articles.title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17B
articles.author: Aisha Malik
articles.content:
DoorDash announced on Thursday that it has agreed to acquire rival Instacart for $17 billion. The acquisition would bring two major players in on-demand delivery under one roof, combining DoorDash’s dominance in restaurant takeout with Instacart’s reach in grocery delivery.

DoorDash will buy Instacart for a total value of $65 for each Instacart share, the company said. The deal has been approved by the boards of both companies.

“Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Instacart CEO Chris Rogersin a press release.

“When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash’s global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners, offer an even better experience for customers and shoppers, and deliver compelling value for our shareholders.”

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app. The company also notes that the two brands will continue to operate as separate and independent companies until the transaction closes.

DoorDash says the deal could help more grocers build out their own online ordering platforms and advertising businesses using Instacart’s technology, while grocers could also use DoorDash’s fulfillment services to handle more online orders and offer lower-cost delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the press release.

“Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts. Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery. It’s still early innings, but we know that when more people shop local, more dollars stay local,” said Xu.

Instacart currently has a market cap of more than $13 billion, and its stock price is up 25% for the year to date. The company likely viewed this as an opportune time to sell at a desirable price, ahead of intensifying competition in the grocery delivery market.

Bloomberg previously reported that Instacart was in talks with Uber, but that the company hadwalked awayfrom discussions.

The deal is expected to close toward the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.

articles.title: Upwind raises $400M after walking away from Datadog acquisition offer
articles.author: Marina Temkin
articles.content:
Upwind, a San Francisco startup that uses AI to secure cloud infrastructure, has raised a $400 million Series C round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from existing backers including Greylock Partners and Craft Ventures.

The round comes nine months after Upwind closed its previous $250 million financing at a$1.5 billion valuation.

The fresh funding, which has been in the works for months, nearly fell apart after Datadog attempted to buy the company, according to a person familiar with Upwind. Datadog is a publicly traded company that sells tools for monitoring how software runs, known as observability. It didn’t offer a premium above the $3.8 billion valuation set by venture capital investors, the person said, so Upwind decided to stay independent.

Four-year-old Upwind has grown rapidly amid rising AI-driven cybersecurity threats. The startup has been adding $20 million to $30 million in annualized recurring revenue (ARR) each quarter and is projected to end the year at roughly $90 million, according to a person familiar with Upwind’s financials. That means that VCs and Datadog valued the startup at more than 40 times its forecast ARR, a common yardstick for pricing software companies. The high multiple is also well below the 80x ARR fetched by Cyera, another fast-growing cybersecurity startup, according toTechCrunch reportingfrom earlier this year.

Cybersecurity is poised to be the third big wave of AI software that companies will pay for after AI coding tools and customer support, Theory Ventures general partner Tomasz Tunguzrecently wrotein his widely read blog.

By walking away from an acquisition offer, Upwind clearly believes that the company will ultimately be worth more than the $3.8 billion that Datadog was ready to pay for it. However, given how few cybersecurity companies have gone public in recent years, an eventual sale remains the most likely outcome for the startup.

Upwind continues to draw acquisition interest, according to a person familiar with the company.

The startup was founded by Amiram Shachar, whosoldhis previous company, the cloud spend management startup Spot.io, to NetApp for $450 million. Upwind calls its approach to thwarting threats “runtime” security, which means it alerts and remedies attacks and vulnerabilities in active services in real time.

TechCrunch has reached out to both Upwind and Datadog for comment.

articles.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying
articles.author: Tim Fernholz
articles.content:
The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026.

Anthropic has focused on gettingenterprise users to stick aroundand Wednesdayannounceda new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend.

Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results.

This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending.

Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI.

Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released anew report yesterdaybased on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost.

“Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch.  We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.”

Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers.

“It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own — this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.”

It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. These new reporting tools can be seen as a kind of FDE-lite, a lighter version of that hands-on help, for Anthropic customers.

“We’re at a point now where it’s mature enough, where once you’re in, it’s going to be harder and harder to switch because you’ve spent the effort,” he said. “Even if they’re all mostly the same, they’re all going to be slightly different, have their own slight quirks of how they handle agent.md files, etc., and so that cost to switch is not zero.”

articles.title: Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro pushes laptop pricing to a new extreme
articles.author: Lauren Forristal
articles.content:
Apple has officially entered thetouchscreen MacBook Proera, and apparently, it wants to drain your wallet while it’s at it.

The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, which is already a hefty price tag in this economy. But if you want the absolute top-of-the-line model with every possible upgrade, prepare to cough up around $14,549.

AsMacRumorsfirst reported, Apple’sconfiguratorprices the fully loaded 14-inch model at $14,249 and the 16-inch version at $14,549. Both come equipped with Apple’s top-tier M5 Max chip, featuring an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU.

You can blame the ongoing memory shortage and AI’s seemingly endless appetite for hardware for some of the pricing pressure. Moving to a 4TB SSD costs an additional $1,000, while upgrading to 8TB adds $3,000. Want the new 16TB option? That’ll set you back another $7,000.

Another $2,000 gets you 128GB of memory, while nano-texture glass adds $150.

For some perspective, the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro topped out at $10,149. The new model raises that ceiling by a whopping $4,400.

Absurd prices aside, the launch marks a significant shift for Apple, nearly a decade after it first experimented with theTouch Bar. The company eventuallyabandonedthat feature, but now it’s ready to embrace a touchscreen MacBook Pro.

Preorders open October 30, with availability beginning November 6.

articles.title: AI execs may be too out of touch to build for the general public
articles.author: Amanda Silberling
articles.content:
Former Yahoo CEO and early Google engineer Marissa Mayer is catching a lot of flak for how she uses AI. Inan interviewabout her new appDazzle, an AI assistant that learns from your camera roll, Mayer poses what she believes is an impressive flex for the product: It helped her come up with three bullet points about her 10-year-old daughter for a birthday presentation at school, describing her as “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover.”

It’s a vague description, like a generic horoscope — it could probably describe a lot of 10-year-olds.

Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg,marveledthat “the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity.”

"She thought it was perfect."www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/s…

Perhaps Mayer drew so much backlash because we have repeatedly observed sheltered billionaires suggest that we outsourcechild-rearing— one of life’s greatest tests of patience, humility, and kindness — to a computer that isincapable of understandinghuman emotion.

We’ve been primed for this frustration. Last year, OpenAI CEO Sam AltmantoldBored Ape ownerand late night host Jimmy Fallon on national television, “I cannot imagine … figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT.” The public didn’t love that comment, either, but Altman wasn’t fazed by thenegativefeedback. A few months ago, he said on X that a “cool use case” of ChatGPT Work would be creating a podcast that talks about your kids’ upcoming birthdays or soccer games and “explain[s] your kids’ interests.” (He was brutallyratioedwithcommentslike, “What if you just talked to your children?”)

After publication, Mayer defended herself in a longX post. She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do — it resurfaced photos of “forgotten kindergarten projects,” like a “snake devenomer” or “sandcat playground,” illustrating her daughter’s creativity and care for animals.

Fair enough. But Mayerremarksin the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of “figuring out the theme for your child’s birthday party.” She says she’s used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband’s AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it’s depressing to imagine this “frictionless future … planned by AI,” Mayer replies, “I haven’t really thought that through.”

These leaders seem to write off the naysayers as part of a small, angry fringe group. Yet a Pew Research Centerstudyreports that 50% of U.S. adults think that AI will reduce people’s ability to form meaningful relationships. Only 5% of respondents said AI would make it easier to build these connections.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, however, joins his Silicon Valley kin in envisioning a world where our social needs are met via AI.

“The average American I think has, it’s fewer than three friends, three people they’d consider friends, and the average person has demand for meaningfully more, I think it’s like 15 friends,” Zuckerberg said last year on apodcast. “The average person wants more connectivity, connection than they have.”

Zuckerberg predicts that it will become more socially acceptable to outsource our emotional needs to AI therapists or even AI romantic partners. “There are all these things that are better about physical connections when you can have them,” he added. “But the reality is that people … feel more alone a lot of the time than they would like.”

Zuckerberg goes on to explain how virtual-reality embodiments of AI avatars are only growing more realistic. Meta seems to be more keen on improving our relationships with these approximations of humans, rather than between the actual billions of humans who use its platforms each day.

Maybe part of this stems from the culture of the tech industry, which prizes efficiency. People try to biohack their own bodies by optimizing theirsleep scheduleswith health trackers or injecting unregulated “peptide stacks” to maximize their productivity.

If you’re building electric vehicles or computer chips, then sure, efficiency is a clear north star. But our relationships with other people are not a tech product that we’ve been challenged to ship with as little capital as possible. Human relationships are inherently messy, but our connections with one another can be what gives our lives meaning. When we delegate those interactions to computers, we surrender the difficult, yet fulfilling experience of being people.

articles.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
articles.author: Rebecca Bellan
articles.content:
Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in aregulatory filingon Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasinglycompetefor thesame customers.

(Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.)

For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.

Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.

It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’srevenue from OpenAIcame from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunchreported, citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year.

OpenAIreportedlyshares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.

Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September. That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

articles.title: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
articles.author: Marina Temkin
articles.content:
Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Alder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mather served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together.

Despite having no direct background in architecture, Alder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than afew decades ago, as development costs have surged.

“We’ve gone from dial-up internet to super intelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch.

Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to buildDream, a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit.

If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part-by-part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.”

While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s built world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.

“Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said.

The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC.

Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California.

While Dream isn’t the only company trying to update AEC software with AI, other startups working on this include Motif, Snaptrude, and Arcol—Elder and Mathur claim they are the only ones that developed a built world model that instantly designs whole buildings.

Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.”

articles.title: SuperMe raises $20M for its network of AI expert profiles
articles.author: Ivan Mehta
articles.content:
When people have career or job questions, they usually tap into their network to find experts who’ve faced a similar predicament and can offer answers. Increasingly, that job is falling to AI.

SuperMe is a network of AI profiles built from the knowledge of real-life experts. When you ask a question, the platform determines which experts are best suited to answer and creates a group chat with their AI profiles.

To scale that network on both sides, meaning more users asking questions and more experts supplying knowledge, the startup announced today that it is raising $20 million in funding led by Kirsten Green at Forerunner, with participation from Greylock Partners.

Casey Winters and Ludo Antonov founded the startup in 2024. Both have experience at large consumer companies. Winters held exec roles at Grubhub, Pinterest, and Eventbrite, and has advised companies like Airbnb and Canva part time. Antonov was head of engineering at multiple startups, including Pinterest, Lyft, and Whatnot.

The two got connected when Winters was advising Whatnot. ChatGPT was becoming popular around the same time, and they decided to build a network business using AI.

“There are these hidden networks in Silicon Valley of who the best people are for niche skills. Our idea was: could we make that network of who the absolute best people are more transparent, and could we take all of the key insights that are locked inside their heads and make them more readily available?” Winters told TechCrunch over a call.

Users can go to the SuperMe website and type their question into the chatbot to start a group of experts. They can also return to a group they have formed or joined and ask follow-up questions.

You can ask a question like “Analyze my pitch deck. Which parts of the story are the weakest,and which questions should I be most prepared to answer?” and get answers from AI profiles of longtime VCs like Mercedes Bent, Sarah Tavel, and Josh Elman. Users can also go to these people’s profiles and ask questions directly rather than in a group chat.

To collect knowledge from users, SuperMe scans public sources such as LinkedIn, YouTube, Substack, and blogs. It also draws on connected apps such as Google Drive, Notion, Gmail, and meeting notetaking tools like Granola. SuperMe said some of this data will include personal information and trade secrets, but it makes sure that none of it appears in answers.

The network is currently free, but the startup plans to cap the number of questions users can ask, after which they will have to cough up some money. It is also considering how to give experts incentives to add more knowledge.

SuperMe also works with MCP (Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI chatbots connect to outside tools and data), so users can ask questions from within chatbots such as Claude and ChatGPT.

The startup has about 13 employees. It is hiring on the tech side to improve its AI models for conversation and for matching questions to experts, and on the network side for someone to find experts in subject areas the platform doesn’t yet cover.

Forerunner’s Green said that SuperMe is well positioned to build a platform where AI collaborates with humans.

“I think it’s one of the reasons why this is very timely, and it’s good to have something like this establishing itself when we’re relatively early in this journey,” she told TechCrunch over a call. “Because there’s going to be so many lessons that are going to be learned, and they need to be shared so that people can come along in a productive way. I think that the balance here is to build a network so that you do have a true sharing component where there are incentives and benefits for everybody to contribute what they know.”
